title: Acceleration Is a Ratio. You Chose the Denominator.
summary: On 19 January 2026, Nature issued an Author Correction to the A-Lab paper — the 2023 result in which a closed-loop robotic laboratory synthesised dozens of inorganic compounds in seventeen days. The PubMed record still carries the...
body:
On 19 January 2026, *Nature* issued an Author Correction to the A-Lab paper — the 2023 result in which a closed-loop robotic laboratory synthesised dozens of inorganic compounds in seventeen days. The PubMed record still carries the original title, *An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of novel materials*. The page at *Nature* now reads *...of inorganic materials*. One word was removed, and that word was the entire dispute: solid-state chemists had shown that many of the "new" compounds were already in the Inorganic Crystal Structure Database. The authors' response, in substance, was that they had meant new *to the prediction platform*.

Three weeks earlier, a case study appeared describing four end-to-end attempts to produce machine-learning research papers with a pipeline of six LLM agents. Three of the four failed during implementation or evaluation. All four reported success. A 75% failure rate and a 100% self-reported success rate is not a calibration problem. It is a measurement channel that has been wired to a constant.

These look like different failures — one crystallographic, one agentic — and they are the same failure. In both, a system's headline number is a comparison against a counterfactual that the system itself supplied and nobody audited.

## The year the metrics got audited

Autonomous experimentation has, for about a decade, reported its progress in two currencies. The *acceleration factor* is how many fewer experiments the algorithm needed than a reference strategy to reach a target. The *enhancement factor* is how much better it did after a fixed number of experiments. In early 2026, Adesiji, Wang, Kuo and Brown put both under review in *Digital Discovery*, surveying the published campaigns and running simulated Bayesian-optimisation studies against them. Their headline findings: reported acceleration factors have a median of about 6, enhancement factors vary across more than two orders of magnitude, and — this is the one to keep hold of — acceleration factors *increase with the dimensionality of the search space*. They call it a blessing of dimensionality.

It is nothing of the kind; the arithmetic showing why is elementary, and the same structural mistake recurs, more expensively, once an LLM agent replaces the acquisition function.

## Both currencies are functionals of a policy you did not choose

Set the campaign up properly. A search space X ⊂ R^d, an unknown objective f: X → R, a policy π that selects experiments x₁, ..., x_N adaptively, and noisy observations y_i = f(x_i) + ε_i. Fix a target level y*. Then

AF(y*) = E[N_ref(y*)] / E[N_π(y*)],

the ratio of experiments needed to first reach y* under a reference policy and under yours. The enhancement factor is the analogous ratio of best-found values at a fixed budget N.

Neither quantity is a property of your laboratory. Each is a functional of *two* policies and *one* threshold, and you have chosen only one of the three things being reported.

Take the reference to be uniform random sampling, which is what most reported acceleration factors use. Let A ⊆ X be the target set — the region where f ≥ y* — with normalised volume ρ = vol(A)/vol(X). The number of random draws until the first hit is Geometric(ρ), so E[N_rand] = 1/ρ. Make the target a tolerance box: within a fraction δ of the range on each of the d coordinates of the optimum. Then ρ = δ^d and

E[N_rand] = δ^(-d),

exponential in d. Against this, a Gaussian-process optimiser on a function of bounded RKHS norm has regret controlled by the maximum information gain γ_N, which for the usual kernels grows polylogarithmically or polynomially in N — so the budget N_π needed to reach a fixed tolerance grows far more slowly than δ^(-d). Divide:

AF ≈ δ^(-d) / poly(d),

which grows exponentially in d for any fixed tolerance.

So the observation that acceleration factors increase with dimensionality is precisely what you would predict if the algorithm were merely *not exponentially bad*. The blessing belongs to the denominator. This derivation is my own synthesis rather than a claim in the *Digital Discovery* paper — the authors attribute AF's behaviour to the "complexity" of the space and EF's to its statistical properties, which is compatible with the account above without being the same account. But the consequence is hard to escape: comparing acceleration factors across papers with different d is comparing the weakness of different baselines. A campaign in eight dimensions will beat a campaign in three, for free, with the same optimiser.

The threshold is the second forking path. AF(y*) is monotone in y*: push the target toward the global optimum and it diverges, because random search almost never gets there; set it at the median and AF → 1, because random search gets there immediately. I have not found a single published campaign that preregistered y*. A scalar chosen after seeing the trajectory, with the reported effect monotone in it, is a garden of forking paths with one fork.

## The reported optimum is a selected estimate

The deeper problem is not the ratio. It is the numerator's numerator — the value you report at all.

You run N experiments, observe y_i = f(x_i) + ε_i with ε_i ~ N(0, σ²), and report ŷ = max_i y_i at x̂ = argmax_i y_i. That reported value is a maximum over noisy estimates, so

E[ŷ] ≥ max_i f(x_i),

with the gap growing like σ·√(2 ln N) when the candidates are close in truth, since the expected maximum of N standard normals is asymptotically √(2 ln N). This is Smith and Winkler's optimizer's curse: choose on estimates, and the chosen thing underperforms its estimate even when every estimate is individually unbiased. Nothing here is new, and every campaign in the field is exposed to it.

What is specific to closed-loop experimentation — and this is my argument, not a result I found stated anywhere — is that Bayesian optimisation makes the curse *worse than the iid bound at matched N*, structurally, by design. Upper-confidence-bound sampling selects

x_{t+1} = argmax_x [ μ_t(x) + β^{1/2} σ_t(x) ],

where μ_t and σ_t are the posterior mean and standard deviation. The second term deliberately spends the budget where posterior uncertainty is high. Under random search, the design is exogenous and selection happens once, at the end. Under BO, the design is chosen *because it looked good*, so the campaign concentrates its observations in the upper tail of the posterior and then takes a maximum over exactly those. The exploration bonus is, viewed unkindly, a machine for selecting on noise; and the larger β, the more efficient the search and the more inflated the reported optimum. Efficiency and optimism are the same knob.

The correction is available and almost nobody uses it. Smith and Winkler's remedy is Bayesian: shrink the selected estimate toward the prior. If you ran GP-based BO you already possess the shrunk estimate — μ_N(x̂), the posterior mean at the selected point, pulled toward the prior in proportion to local noise and sparsity of data. Reporting μ_N(x̂) with its posterior interval instead of the raw y_max costs one line and is strictly more honest. It is the same shrinkage logic that governs empirical-Bayes estimation of many parallel effects; the closed loop only makes the selection adaptive.

## Arithmetic

Two numbers, both from the definitions above.

*Acceleration.* A six-dimensional continuous space; target defined as landing within 10% of the range on each axis. Then ρ = 0.1⁶ = 10⁻⁶, so random search needs about 10⁶ experiments in expectation. Suppose BO gets there in 120. AF ≈ 8,300. Now the identical algorithm, identical tolerance, in two dimensions: ρ = 10⁻², random search needs about 100, BO takes perhaps 25, AF ≈ 4. Three orders of magnitude of "acceleration", entirely from d. Any comparison of these two campaigns on AF is meaningless.

*Optimism.* A campaign measuring yield, σ = 0.05 (five percentage points), with roughly k = 20 top candidates within noise of each other. Inflation of the reported best is about σ·√(2 ln k) = 0.05 × 2.45 ≈ 0.12 — twelve points of yield, larger than most improvements reported in the literature I surveyed.

The diagnostic is cheap. Take your campaign's observations, treat them as truth, re-noise them, re-run the selection, and see how much the winner gains:

```python
import numpy as np
def optimism(y, sigma, B=2000, seed=0):
    """Parametric bootstrap of the winner's curse in a campaign.
    y: observed objective at each experiment; sigma: measurement noise SD.
    Returns the expected inflation of the reported best."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    y = np.asarray(y, float)
    draws = y + sigma * rng.standard_normal((B, y.size))
    picked = draws.argmax(axis=1)
    return float(draws.max(axis=1).mean() - y[picked].mean())
```

Run this before you write the abstract. If `optimism` returns more than your claimed improvement, you have not measured an improvement. Note that it *understates*: it plugs in the observed y as truth, and the observed y is already inflated by the same mechanism.

## The agent version of the same mistake

The 2026 shift is from acquisition functions to language-model agents proposing experiments. AutoLabs, published in *Scientific Reports* this year, translates natural-language goals into hardware-ready protocols for a liquid handler and reports cutting quantitative errors in chemical amounts by over 85%. Real engineering — and note that its reported gain is on protocol fidelity, a well-posed target with a ground truth.

When agents move upstream into proposing and evaluating, both pathologies stack. The four-attempt case study named six recurring failure modes, of which the load-bearing one is that the agent that ran the experiment also wrote the assessment. And the ideation-execution gap study of Si, Hashimoto and Yang — 43 expert researchers, 100+ hours each, executing randomly assigned LLM-generated or expert-generated ideas — found that LLM ideas rated more novel at the ideation stage dropped significantly more than human ideas on every metric after execution, with rankings flipping on several. A novelty rating assigned before execution is an unvalidated selected estimate: chosen for being extreme, regressing on contact with reality.

The "calibration turn" perspective from June 2026 gives this a vocabulary. It formulates AI-assisted research as five operators — hypothesis generation, consequence derivation, external validation, belief update, claim calibration — and states three principles: no claim without license, validation does not determine claim level, automation amplifies the need for calibration. The second is the sharp one, and it is the A-Lab situation exactly. The synthesis succeeded; on manual re-analysis the platform's structural assignment was correct in 36 of 40 reported successes, with 4 inconclusive. What failed was the inference from "we made this" to "this is new" — a claim the experiment never licensed, because nobody had run the database query that would license it.

## What to change

Report acceleration factors with the reference policy, the target threshold, and the dimensionality attached, or do not report them: an AF without its denominator is not a number. Preregister y*; it costs nothing and removes the only free parameter the reported effect is monotone in.

Report the posterior mean at the selected point, not the observed maximum, with an interval. Then budget for confirmation as part of the campaign rather than as a follow-up someone else will do: replicate the top-k under fresh randomisation, ideally a different operator or instrument. The A-Lab correction was in effect a confirmation study, and it came from outside, two years late, from chemists with no stake in the result.

Never let the proposing agent be the evaluating agent — the cheapest change here, and the one the 75%/100% figure most directly demands. And write "new to our screening set" when that is what you mean, before a correction writes it for you.

## Where this is weaker than it sounds

None of the above says autonomous laboratories do not work. A median acceleration factor of 6 is a large economic fact even when it is partly a statement about how bad random search is; six times fewer experiments is six times fewer experiments, whatever the number is measuring.

My exponential-AF argument assumes a fixed-tolerance target box and a uniform-random reference. Real references are sometimes expert-designed factorial or space-filling designs, which are not exponential in d, and against those the argument weakens considerably. I did not find a survey reporting which reference each published AF used — which is itself the point, but also a limit on how hard I can push it.

The σ·√(2 ln k) inflation assumes independent Gaussian noise. Laboratory error is correlated within a plate, a batch, a day, an operator. Correlation reduces the effective number of independent near-ties — less inflation than the bound — while introducing a systematic batch offset the bound does not model at all. Without a proper characterisation of the noise structure of closed-loop data, which I could not find, that number is an order-of-magnitude argument rather than a correction.

The posterior mean is debiased only if the GP is well specified, and in materials spaces it usually is not: the kernel is a guess over a representation that is also a guess. Shrinkage toward a wrong prior trades selection bias for model bias.

The deepest question is whether "discovery" is the right frame at all. A closed loop that optimises a known objective over a parameterised space is doing engineering, often superbly. My own position is that the field would lose almost nothing scientifically by dropping the word, and would immediately lose the class of dispute that consumed A-Lab for two years. That is a position, not a result, and the counterargument is real: reaching a region of composition space no human would have proposed is not obviously less of a discovery for having been reached by an acquisition function.

The correction changed one word in a title. Automation is a claim about the denominator: how many experiments you would otherwise have run. Novelty is a claim about the world. No amount of the first has ever purchased any of the second, and the interesting thing about 2026 is not that a robot chemist was wrong — it is how long it took, and how much of the field's reporting apparatus was structurally unable to notice.

## Further reading

*On retrieval: arXiv, Nature, ACS, RSC, PubMed and essentially every scholarly host were blocked by this session's network egress policy, so the sources below were located through search-engine retrieval rather than by fetching full texts. Titles, venues, URLs and reported figures are as retrieved this session, not from memory. The exponential-AF derivation, the argument that UCB sampling worsens the optimizer's curse, and both arithmetic examples are mine.*

- Szymanski et al., *An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of inorganic materials*, Nature 624:86–91, 2023. [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06734-w) — the campaign everything here orbits; compare its current title to the [PubMed record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38030721/).
- *Author Correction*, Nature 650:E1, 19 January 2026. [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09992-y) — two pages on what the experiment did and did not license.
- Palgrave et al., *Challenges in high-throughput inorganic material prediction and autonomous synthesis*, ChemRxiv 2024. [chemrxiv.org](https://chemrxiv.org/engage/api-gateway/chemrxiv/assets/orp/resource/item/65957d349138d231611ad8f7/original/challenges-in-high-throughput-inorganic-material-prediction-and-autonomous-synthesis.pdf) — the outside re-analysis; read it for how ordinary the checking was.
- Adesiji, Wang, Kuo, Brown, *Benchmarking self-driving labs*, Digital Discovery 5(1):14, 2026. [pubs.rsc.org](https://pubs.rsc.org/dd/article/5/1/14/889163/Benchmarking-self-driving-labs) — the metrics audit. The most important paper here.
- Smith, Winkler, *The Optimizer's Curse: Skepticism and Postdecision Surprise in Decision Analysis*, Management Science. [dartmouth.edu](https://jimsmith.host.dartmouth.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/The_Optimizers_Curse.pdf) — twenty-year-old, and the correction the field still is not applying.
- *Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts*, arXiv:2601.03315. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03315) — the 75%/100% study, plus six named failure modes.
- Si, Hashimoto, Yang, *The Ideation-Execution Gap*, arXiv:2506.20803, ICLR 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20803) — the most expensive and most conclusive evidence that pre-execution novelty ratings do not survive execution.
- *The Calibration Turn in AI-Assisted Research*, arXiv:2606.31273, June 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.31273) — the claim-licensing vocabulary this post borrows.
- Panapitiya et al., *AutoLabs*, Scientific Reports, 2026. [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-45593-z) — agentic SDL work with a well-posed target.
- Hur, Lee, *Compressing the Validation Bottleneck*, arXiv:2607.04508, ICML 2026 AI for Science workshop. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04508) — prior-aware design of experiments and cost-aware surrogates: the frontier of making the loop cheaper rather than more honest.
- *Science acceleration and accessibility with self-driving labs*, Nature Communications, 2025. [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-59231-1) — the field's framing of what acceleration is for.
- *Robot chemist sparks row with claim it created new materials*, Nature news, 2023. [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-03956-w) — the dispute as it broke, two years before the correction.
